"The Council has not merely concealed the origins of the First Gate. It has altered the rituals used to maintain it. The Elders have been drawing power from the bloodline custodians while presenting the process as necessary maintenance."

He opens a second document.

"These are the extraction records from the last three generations. The quantities were increased without the knowledge of the participating families. Several entries record failed procedures and permanent injuries. Others refer to children being transferred between houses to preserve the continuity of the bloodline."

The chamber erupts.

Representatives begin speaking over one another. Some demand explanations. Others turn towards the Elders with open anger.

Corvin strikes his staff against the floor.

"Enough!"

The chamber falls silent, but the obedience is no longer automatic.

"You are allowing yourselves to be manipulated," he says. "The Gate is unstable. Without the Council's authority, the binding will fail. Everything we have preserved will be lost."

You step forward.

"The Gate does not need your authority. It needs the original warding sequence restored and the corrupted channels removed."

Marek looks towards you.

You know what he is thinking. The evidence is powerful, but evidence alone will not dismantle the Council. They need to show the representatives that the Elders' control is no longer necessary.

You place your palm against the central table.

Your bloodline resonance spreads through the carved iron.

The chamber's old wards awaken.

Silver lines appear beneath the floor, revealing the network that connects the Council chamber to the First Gate. The Elders' individual sigils glow in response, but several begin to flicker.

You direct a controlled pulse through the structure.

The connection between the Gate and the Council's command seals breaks.

One by one, the iron crests above the Elders go dark.

A shocked silence follows.

Corvin stares at the dead sigils.

"What have you done?"

"Removed your authority to command the Gate."

***

The reaction is immediate.

Two Elders stand and attempt to restore their connections. Their spells reach towards the floor, but the ancient network no longer answers them.

Marek raises one hand.

Iron bands rise around the central dais, preventing anyone from reaching the old control mechanisms.

"Do not make this worse," he says.

Corvin turns on him.

"You would betray everything you have served?"

Marek's expression changes.

For the first time since you have known him, the careful composure of the First Scholar disappears.

"I served the Coven because I believed its knowledge protected people. I defended its borders, trained its soldiers and enforced its laws. I believed the restrictions existed because some magic was too dangerous to be shared."

He looks at the register.

"But you did not preserve knowledge. You hoarded it. You did not protect the bloodline custodians. You exploited them."

Corvin's voice becomes cold.

"You owe your position to this Council."

"I know."

"Your authority, your education, your entire life—"

"Was built upon information you deliberately withheld."

Marek lowers his hand.

"I will not defend that any longer."

A representative from House Veyr steps away from the Elders' side. Two more follow. Then a military commander removes the silver badge of Council authority from his coat and places it on the table.

The fracture spreads.

Some representatives remain loyal, unwilling to abandon the institution that has given their houses influence and security. Others openly demand the Elders surrender their positions. Several senior scholars ask for access to the original archives.

The Council is no longer a single body.

Its members are choosing sides.

Corvin looks around the chamber and finally understands.

He has lost the obedience that made his position powerful.

***

The confrontation lasts for hours.

There are arguments, accusations and attempts to negotiate. The Elders demand that the First Gate be returned to their control. The witch houses refuse to accept another binding agreement without independent review.

Marek uses his military standing to prevent the loyalist factions from turning the dispute into violence. Officers who once followed his orders now stand between the Elders and the representatives.

You remain beside the register.

Every time someone questions the records, you show them the evidence. Every time an Elder claims the bloodline rituals were necessary, you explain how the original system functioned before the Council altered it.

You do not promise that the Gate will be easy to maintain.

You do not pretend that the ancient magic is harmless.

You simply refuse to let fear become an excuse for ownership.

By evening, the Elders have lost control of the chamber.

Three resign their positions rather than face formal investigation. Two are removed by a vote of the remaining representatives. Corvin refuses to surrender his authority, but without the command seals or the support of the witch houses, his orders carry little weight.

The Council's power is broken.

Not destroyed, but stripped of the mechanisms that allowed it to rule without question.

A temporary assembly is established, with representatives from each major house and independent scholars appointed to review the First Gate. The original records are copied and distributed to the houses. The remaining bloodline custodians are to be informed of their history and given the right to refuse further participation in the rituals.

It is an imperfect beginning.

But it is a beginning.

***

You find Marek alone in the archive gallery after midnight.

He stands before the shelves where he spent much of his life studying. The familiar books are arranged exactly as they were yesterday, but the place feels different now.

"They will remember this as a betrayal," he says.

"Some of them will."

"I spent twenty years earning my position. I believed I was making the Coven stronger."

You stand beside him.

"You did make it stronger."

He looks at you.

"That is not the same as making it right."

"No."

For a moment, neither of you speaks.

Marek removes one of the silver rings from his finger and turns it slowly in his palm.

"I do not know what I am without the Coven."

"You are still the man who learned its secrets."

"That knowledge was given to me by the institution I have just helped dismantle."

"Then decide what to do with it now."

He looks down at the ring.

You understand that abandoning an oppressive institution does not erase the years spent serving it. Marek will have to answer for the orders he gave, the people he controlled and the decisions he made when he still believed the Council's authority was legitimate.

You will not pretend those things no longer matter.

But neither will you pretend that he cannot choose differently.

He places the ring on the shelf.

"I think I would like to teach."

You raise an eyebrow.

"Teach?"

"Without deciding in advance who is permitted to learn."

A faint smile touches your face.

"That would be a start."

***

The following morning, the first meeting of the provisional assembly takes place.

The chamber is less impressive without the Elders seated at its centre. Representatives occupy the benches in small groups, and several scholars have brought stacks of documents to be examined.

There is disagreement almost immediately.

One house wants the First Gate dismantled entirely. Another insists that the old wards must remain under military supervision. A third demands compensation for families whose ancestors were used in the bloodline rituals.

No one has an easy answer.

You sit beside Marek and listen.

The old Council would have resolved such disagreements through authority. The new assembly must learn to resolve them through argument, evidence and compromise.

It will be slower.

It will also be harder to corrupt quietly.

When the discussion turns to the future of the First Gate, you stand.

"The Gate must be maintained, but no bloodline should ever again be treated as its property. Its records must remain accessible. Its rituals must be understood by more than a handful of appointed scholars. Anyone asked to contribute their magic must know what is being asked of them and be free to refuse."

A representative asks, "And who will oversee it?"

You look towards Marek.

"We will establish an independent group of wardens, answerable to the assembly and the people affected by their decisions. No single house will control the process."

There are objections.

There are questions you cannot yet answer.

But nobody dismisses the proposal.

***

Later, you stand with Marek on the balcony overlooking the valley.

The morning light touches the distant mountains. The First Gate remains sealed, its ancient magic quiet beneath the earth. It will need careful attention in the coming months, and the provisional assembly may yet fracture under the weight of competing interests.

The old Council has lost its authority.

That does not mean trust has suddenly returned.

Marek rests his hands on the stone railing.

"They will try to rebuild what we have taken apart."

"Some will."

"Others will claim that the old methods were necessary."

"Then we make sure the records survive."

He looks towards you.

"And if they try to bind another bloodline?"

"Then they will have to answer to everyone who knows what happened to mine."

The words settle between you.

You think of the generations who came before you, people whose names were reduced to entries in a register. They never had the chance to challenge the system that controlled them.

You cannot give them back their choices.

But you can make certain their descendants inherit something different.

Marek takes your hand.

"There is a great deal still to do."

"I know."

"And there will be people who blame us."

"I know that too."

He studies your face.

"Do you regret it?"

You look towards the valley.

"No."

The answer is not triumphal. It carries the weight of everything that has been exposed, and everything that must now be repaired.

The Council is gone as it was.

The witch houses remain divided. The Gate still requires protection. Marek must learn to live without the institution that shaped him, and you must discover who you are when your bloodline is no longer defined by the demands of others.

But the records are open.

The command seals are broken.

And no Elder can quietly order your blood to be taken in the name of tradition.

For generations, your family was made to serve the Council.

Now, for the first time, the future of the Gate belongs to those who choose to protect it.

You turn from the balcony and walk back into the archive beside Marek.

There is work to do.

And this time, the knowledge will belong to everyone.
